findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute without justification
findings.body: The background cleanup ticker is changed from time.Minute*10 to time.Minute*1, so all cleanup jobs including the now multi-query annotation cleanup run 10x more often. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix described in the PR, is not mentioned in the description, and increases steady-state database and CPU load on every Grafana instance. Revert to 10 minutes or justify/configure the change separately.

findings.title: Successful routine cleanup batches are logged at Error level with full ID lists
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 use r.log.Error for normal progress messages on every batch, including batches where err is nil (the fetch error was already returned above) and batches with zero IDs. This will emit error-level logs on every cleanup run, trigger error alerting/log-based monitoring, and include the complete ids slice (bounded only by AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize, e.g. 32767 IDs in the new test), producing huge log lines and I/O overhead. These should be Debug/Info without the full ID list or only logged when an actual error occurs.

findings.title: Placeholder-limit workaround only handles SQLite, leaving large batches broken on PostgreSQL
findings.body: deleteByIDs inlines IDs only when the DB is SQLite and the configured batch size exceeds 999; otherwise it builds one '?' placeholder per ID. PostgreSQL has a 65535 bind-parameter limit (and drivers/DBs have similar limits), so a configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above that limit makes DELETE ... IN (?,...,?) fail with too-many-parameters, whereas the previous single-statement DELETE had no bind parameters and worked for any batch size. The decision is also based on the configured batch size rather than len(ids). Chunk the delete by actual ID count or inline/chunk for all dialects.

findings.title: SQLite ID inlining builds the IN list quadratically
findings.body: For SQLite batches over 999, values is rebuilt with fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) for every ID, copying the entire accumulated string each iteration. With the tested batch size of 32767 (and larger allowed configurations) this is O(n^2) copying and allocations on the cleanup path. Build the list with strings.Builder / strconv instead.
